title: A Simple Weekly Review for Technical Work
content:
By Friday, the code may be merged while the important uncertainty remains untouched. A weekly technical review should reveal that difference. Its output is a short record of what changed, what evidence exists, where work is stuck, and which few actions deserve the next week. It is not an exercise in proving that every hour was busy.

Collect evidence before judging the week

Open the issue tracker, calendar, deployment notes, and personal task list. Capture unfinished commitments as well as completed ones. Write each item as an outcome or decision, not an activity label. “Investigated cache” is hard to evaluate; “confirmed stale responses originate at the proxy cache” says what changed in understanding. If the origin is still uncertain, say so.

Keep evidence links beside the statement: a reviewed change, a reproducible defect, a screenshot of an accepted design, or a short experiment report. A link is more useful than a long retrospective written from memory. Do not place sensitive customer data into a general weekly note simply because it helps explain a problem. Link to an appropriately restricted record instead.

GitHub documents milestones as groups of issues and pull requests with progress and due-date information. Such a view is a useful collection surface, but closed-item percentage is not a quality verdict. A small issue and a difficult migration can each count as one item. Use the list to prompt review, not to rank people.

Ask four different questions

First, what reached an observable outcome? Second, what became better understood? Third, what remains blocked and by whom? Fourth, what repeated work should be removed or simplified? Separating these questions prevents a week of valuable investigation from looking empty while also preventing endless investigation from escaping scrutiny.

For every active uncertainty, write the smallest observation that would change the next decision. If a page is slow, that might be a trace of a representative request rather than an immediate rewrite. If a library seems unsuitable, it might be checking one mandatory feature in official documentation. The review should convert vague discomfort into a bounded evidence-gathering step.

Notice toil without treating all operations as waste

The Google SRE chapter on eliminating toil describes operational work with characteristics such as repetition, manual effort, and limited enduring value. Use that distinction carefully. Responding to a new incident can produce valuable learning; repeatedly copying the same report by hand may be a better automation candidate. An unpleasant task is not automatically toil, and an automated task is not automatically well designed.

Keep a small friction log during the week: operation, frequency, failure consequence, and available workaround. At review time, pick one recurring burden worth changing. Estimate the maintenance responsibility as well as time spent. An automation that requires constant repair may move effort instead of removing it. A simpler checklist or better default can sometimes be the more durable improvement.

A hypothetical API maintenance week

Suppose a hypothetical developer planned three outcomes: fix duplicate email notifications, document a webhook contract, and investigate slow exports. By review time, the notification fix is merged and verified against a synthetic duplicate delivery. The webhook document exists but has not been reviewed by its consumer. Export latency is still unresolved because the developer lacks representative timing information.

The review records these as complete, waiting for consumer review, and evidence missing. It does not call all three complete because code or prose was produced. For the webhook, the next action is a named review request with a specific question about retry behavior. For exports, the next action is an approved timing capture that excludes record contents. These actions are narrow enough to finish and inspect.

The friction log also shows the developer manually assembling the same status report on three occasions. Rather than building a large dashboard, the developer first creates one saved tracker view. Whether that change helps would need to be checked in a later review. This hypothetical example supplies no productivity statistics and makes no claim that a particular review cadence works for every team.

Choose commitments that fit the actual week

Check meetings, leave, on-call responsibilities, and external dependencies before selecting next week's outcomes. Preserve room for interruption if operational work is part of the role. Do not plan every available hour as if uncertainty were an exception. A useful commitment names a finish condition and a dependency; it does not require pretending the duration is known precisely.

Limit the review note to what a teammate needs to coordinate: outcomes, evidence, blockers, risks, and next actions. Store detailed debugging notes elsewhere. If the same blocker appears for several reviews, escalate the dependency or revise the plan instead of copying the same sentence indefinitely. The repeated blocker is information about the system of work, not automatically an individual failure.

Review previous commitments at the start of the next cycle. If they changed, record why: new evidence, a higher-priority incident, a missing dependency, or a poor estimate. This makes adaptation visible without turning the note into a performance defense. The proposed structure is an editorial working method, and teams should change it when it stops producing useful decisions.

Weekly technical review checklist

  • Gather open commitments before relying on memory.
  • Attach evidence to delivered outcomes and newly learned facts.
  • Give each blocker a responsible party and next request.
  • Pick one recurring friction worth simplifying.
  • Check next week's real capacity and dependencies.
  • Write finish conditions rather than vague activity goals.
  • Revisit last week's decisions and explain meaningful changes.
excerpt: Run a weekly technical review that separates delivered outcomes, useful learning, blockers, and repetitive toil, then turns them into realistic next actions.
